title: Subjective Perspective Makes Objective Reality ‘Everywhere Whole’ | NOEMA
gist: Reporting from a Berggruen Institute workshop in Venice (Aug. 4, 2026), Nathan Gardels surveys religious scholars, philosophers, a quantum physicist and a neuroscientist who converge, from very different traditions, on the view that there is no metaphysical gap between subject and object, body and soul — consciousness and the world it discloses are two faces of one 'everywhere whole' reality.

insights.claim: The Berggruen Institute convened religious scholars, philosophers, quantum physicists, AI technologists, neuroscientists and science fiction novelists at Casa dei Tre Oci in Venice on Aug. 4, 2026, specifically to debate the nature of consciousness.
insights.speaker: NATHAN GARDELS
insights.so_what: Signals an active, well-funded institutional push (Berggruen Institute) to bring hard science, AI practitioners and metaphysics into direct dialogue — worth tracking as a source of framing for how AI consciousness debates get legitimized in elite policy/ideas circles.
insights.locator: Berggruen Institute gathered religious scholars

insights.claim: The article's framing question — whether there is a metaphysical gap between body and soul, or whether they are the same substance and symbiotic aspects of a singular reality — is presented as a question that recurs across Medieval mystics, ancient 'pagan masters,' and today's quantum physicists and neuroscientists.
insights.speaker: NATHAN GARDELS
insights.so_what: Frames the whole piece as evidence that contemporary science and ancient metaphysics are converging on the same answer rather than diverging — a recurring 'convergence' theme worth watching in Noema's broader editorial line.
insights.quote: whether there is a metaphysical gap between the body and the soul, or if they are made of the same substance, symbiotic aspects of a singular reality that entail each other
insights.locator: The great question then, as now

themes.theme: Mystical and religious models of unified consciousness

insights.claim: The 12th-century text 'Book of 24 Philosophers' (with material attributed to unnamed pagan thinkers from the 3rd-4th centuries), as read by Peter Sloterdijk, describes God as 'an infinite sphere whose center is everywhere and whose circumference is nowhere' — a formless, non-spatial conception of ultimate reality with no inside or outside.
insights.speaker: NATHAN GARDELS
insights.so_what: This is the source of the article's title concept ('everywhere whole') — a recurring mental model in the piece for reality having no privileged outside vantage point, later echoed by both the mystics and the physicist.
insights.quote: God is an infinite sphere whose center is everywhere and whose circumference is nowhere.
insights.locator: Book of 24 Philosophers

insights.claim: Swami Medhananda, a monk of the Ramakrishna Order, coined the term 'polymorphic monism' to describe a non-sectarian reading of Hinduism: one infinite Divine Reality, both personal and impersonal, that can be legitimately known and worshipped through many different names, forms and paths (including forms shared with Islam, Sikhism and Christianity).
insights.speaker: NATHAN GARDELS
insights.so_what: A named, exportable framework — 'polymorphic monism' — distinguishing monism from monotheism; useful shorthand for anyone tracking how pluralist religious frameworks are being formally articulated for cross-tradition dialogue.
insights.quote: I have coined the term polymorphic monism: Hinduism affirms one infinite Divine Reality that can be known and worshipped in many forms.
insights.locator: Swami Medhananda, a monk of the Ramakrishna Order

insights.claim: Medhananda cites the Rig Veda line 'ekam sad viprā bahudhā vadanti' ('Truth is one; the wise call it by many names') as the scriptural root of Hindu pluralism about the divine.
insights.speaker: NATHAN GARDELS
insights.so_what: A concrete textual anchor for the pluralist-monist thesis running through the piece; useful citation for anyone building a comparative-religion argument about unity-in-diversity.
insights.quote: Truth is one; the wise call it by many names.
insights.locator: A celebrated verse from the 'Rig Veda'

insights.claim: Meister Eckhart, the 14th-century Christian mystic, interpreted the incarnation of the divine (the Logos/Word of Genesis and John) not as a one-time historical event in Christ's birth, but as an ongoing process in which humans continuously participate in and conjoin with the unfolding mind of God, becoming 'co-essences' with the divine.
insights.speaker: NATHAN GARDELS
insights.so_what: Positions Christian mysticism as making essentially the same claim as Rovelli's physics later in the piece — that the observer is not outside reality but constitutive of it — reinforcing the article's central convergence thesis.
insights.quote: the incarnation of the divine in man was not a one-time event of Christ’s birth in Bethlehem, but takes place through continuous human participation in the unfolding Logos of the Word
insights.locator: For Eckhart, consciousness was being aware

insights.claim: Sloterdijk's gloss on the mystical tradition is compressed into the aphorism 'to think is to give birth to God,' treating human thought itself as the mechanism by which divine reason (Logos) is continually generated rather than merely observed.
insights.speaker: NATHAN GARDELS
insights.so_what: Encapsulates the piece's throughline that the knowing subject doesn't just perceive reality but actively co-produces it.
insights.quote: To think is to give birth to God.
insights.locator: If God is the pure thought of divine reason

themes.theme: Subjectivity as the fundamental, irreducible ground

insights.claim: Islamic philosopher Muhammed U. Faruque argues, drawing on Sufism, that consciousness is 'self-illuminating and self-cognizing' — it knows itself directly with no subject-object division — and that in the absence of external stimuli, consciousness itself becomes the only 'light' revealing one's presence (ḥuḍūr).
insights.speaker: NATHAN GARDELS
insights.so_what: Sets up a direct philosophical counter to functionalist/behaviorist accounts of mind (relevant to debates about whether an AI system could be 'conscious' through external behavior alone, since Faruque locates consciousness's essence in non-objectifiable presence, not qualia or observable output).
insights.quote: consciousness itself becomes the only ‘light,’ revealing your presence
insights.locator: In the absence of external stimuli

insights.claim: Faruque argues human subjectivity is simultaneously 'empty' (its contents — thoughts, feelings, memories — are not identical with the conscious subject and can change without altering the underlying 'I') and 'total' (every object of experience appears only within consciousness, so the entire universe is disclosed through the knowing subject).
insights.speaker: NATHAN GARDELS
insights.so_what: A specific dual-aspect model of the self (empty + total) that could be cited as a structured alternative to both pure materialist and pure idealist accounts of mind.
insights.quote: Human subjectivity is both empty and total.
insights.locator: Human subjectivity is both empty and total

insights.claim: Faruque contends consciousness must logically precede self-consciousness (I-consciousness in relation to external objects), since a subject must already exist as consciousness before it can become self-aware through contrasting itself with objects — making consciousness more fundamental than reflective or intersubjective experience.
insights.speaker: NATHAN GARDELS
insights.so_what: A causal/ordering claim relevant to any theory (including AI theories of mind) that tries to build consciousness up from object-relations or interaction rather than treating awareness as primary.
insights.locator: There is no reason to think that consciousness comes into existence

insights.claim: Song Bing, president of the Berggruen Institute, argues (via the concept 'Existence,' borrowed from wisdom teacher Liu Fenghe) that because the capacity to perceive stays constant even as the contents of perception constantly change, the underlying perceiver ('I') must itself be unchanging and ever-present — an unarising, unceasing ground from which all perceptual change depends.
insights.speaker: NATHAN GARDELS
insights.so_what: Another named framework ('Existence') paralleling Faruque's 'presence' — shows independent convergence between Islamic and Chinese contemplative traditions on an unchanging-ground theory of the self.
insights.quote: Existence is without arising or ceasing. It inherently possesses all capacity and gives rise to all functioning.
insights.locator: It is what Liu Fenghe

themes.theme: Consciousness as constructed: mirror, hallucination, confabulation

insights.claim: Philosopher Jenann Ismael proposes that consciousness and matter are not competing foundations of reality but the subjective and objective faces of a single existence, illustrated by a mirror: experience is the 'membrane' between an inner and outer world, containing the whole of reality within it while occupying only a thin sliver of that reality by its own account.
insights.speaker: NATHAN GARDELS
insights.so_what: The mirror/membrane metaphor is a reusable mental model for dual-aspect (neither pure idealism nor pure materialism) theories of mind — useful shorthand when comparing competing consciousness frameworks.
insights.quote: it is the membrane between an inner and an outer world, at once containing the whole of reality within it and occupying, by its own account, only a thin sliver of that reality
insights.locator: Picture a mirror on the far wall

insights.claim: Neuroscientist Anil Seth, drawing on roughly 25 years of research, frames the brain as a 'prediction machine' where every conscious experience — of the world or of the self — is a 'controlled hallucination': a brain-based best-guess anchored to reality only via incoming sensory signals, meaning experience is generated as much 'inside out' as 'outside in.'
insights.speaker: NATHAN GARDELS
insights.so_what: The 'controlled hallucination' framework is a well-established but still-debated neuroscience thesis with direct implications for how AI perception/prediction systems are analogized to biological consciousness — worth flagging wherever AI cognition claims lean on predictive-processing analogies.
insights.quote: the brain is a prediction machine, and every conscious experience we have — whether of the world, or of the self — is a kind of controlled hallucination
insights.locator: My own work on consciousness

insights.claim: Science fiction novelist Ken Liu argues consciousness is fundamentally a subjectively experienced state that only the experiencing agent can judge as 'real,' and that reducing it to functional tests, behavioral proxies or neural signatures would define away subjectivity itself, leaving only 'a shadow' rather than consciousness.
insights.speaker: NATHAN GARDELS
insights.so_what: A direct, explicit pushback against functionalist tests for machine consciousness — directly relevant to how AI labs and researchers claim or disclaim consciousness in AI systems based on behavioral benchmarks.
insights.quote: no one can judge whether it is ‘real’ except the agent experiencing it
insights.locator: Since consciousness is a subjectively experienced state

insights.claim: Ken Liu argues that building thinking machines (AI) will nonetheless help humans better understand their own neural circuitry — for example, illuminating 'confabulation' (the brain's active reconstruction of memory and its construction of integrated sensory simultaneity despite differing neural transmission times) — and that this compression-confabulation ability may be essential to whether a finite being can be conscious.
insights.speaker: NATHAN GARDELS
insights.so_what: Frames AI development as an epistemic instrument for consciousness research rather than (or in addition to) an attempt to replicate consciousness — a nuanced, non-obvious framing of AI's scientific value that differs from typical AGI-consciousness debates.
insights.quote: Constructing thinking machines will help us better understand our own neural circuitry.
insights.locator: Constructing thinking machines will help us

themes.theme: Physics against dualism: Rovelli's relational realism

insights.claim: Quantum physicist Carlo Rovelli argues the much-discussed metaphysical gap between body and soul, subjective and objective, does not exist: humans are not observers outside the world but embodied parts of it, and our theories and knowledge are themselves natural phenomena and aspects of the very world they describe, not disembodied views from outside.
insights.speaker: NATHAN GARDELS
insights.so_what: A leading physicist's explicit rejection of Cartesian dualism, framed as consistent with 'everything we have learned about nature in the last centuries' — a strong, citable scientific anchor for arguments against mind-body dualism.
insights.quote: We, subjects of knowledge and understanding, are not outside the world. We are part of it.
insights.locator: As he has written in Noema

insights.claim: Rovelli holds that the mind is simply the behavior of the brain properly described in a high-level language, and that one's own first-person experience of oneself and an external, third-person account of oneself are not primary/secondary but two distinct perspectives on the same underlying events.
insights.speaker: NATHAN GARDELS
insights.so_what: A precise, mechanistic statement of physicalist non-reductionism (mind as high-level description, not eliminated but not separate substance either) — a useful reference point for AI/neuroscience debates about levels of description.
insights.quote: The mind is the behavior of the brain, properly described in a high-level language.
insights.locator: For Rovelli, the notion of a metaphysical gap

insights.claim: Rovelli rejects the demand for any ultimate or fundamental account of reality, arguing every account is approximate, has blind spots, and is itself realized within (embodied in) the very reality it describes — there is no problem with the resulting circularity between epistemology (how we know) and ontology (what exists).
insights.speaker: NATHAN GARDELS
insights.so_what: An epistemic-humility framework applicable beyond physics: no theory (including AI models of mind) can claim a view-from-nowhere, since the theorist is always embedded in what's being theorized about.
insights.locator: Nor do we need to require that there is any ultimate

insights.claim: Rovelli argues explicitly against dualism between animate and inanimate, human and animal, earth and heavens, and soul and body — concluding that once dualism is abandoned, one can speak of soul and emotions as legitimately real as a kitchen table, even though the table is also just a collection of atoms.
insights.speaker: NATHAN GARDELS
insights.so_what: Gives a concrete, almost folk-physics analogy (soul is as real as a kitchen table) for reconciling scientific materialism with talk of spiritual/emotional life — a rhetorically strong bridging device.
insights.quote: Earth is not metaphysically different from the heavens, living beings are not metaphysically different from inanimate matter, humans are not metaphysically different from other animals.
insights.locator: Earth is not metaphysically different

insights.claim: Rovelli declares that 'objectivity without a subject' — the idea of a view of reality from nowhere, with no observer embedded in it — is an abstract construct of little relevance, calling it 'the illusion of a science now belonging to the past.'
insights.speaker: NATHAN GARDELS
insights.so_what: An explicit declaration that the classical scientific ideal of observer-independent objectivity is obsolete — a strong, quotable claim for anyone tracking how physics is repositioning the role of the observer (echoes relational quantum mechanics, Rovelli's own field).
insights.quote: objectivity without a subject is an abstract construct, of little relevance — it is the illusion of a science now belonging to the past
insights.locator: That Medieval insight is another way of saying

themes.theme: The convergence thesis: mysticism and physics arrive at the same place

insights.claim: Gardels explicitly links Rovelli's physics-based rejection of dualism to Meister Eckhart's 14th-century mystical claim that consciousness is awareness of both inhabiting and being inhabited by the mind of God, presenting the two as independent traditions (physics and Christian mysticism) converging on the same conclusion about the constitutive role of the observer.
insights.speaker: NATHAN GARDELS
insights.so_what: The article's core interpretive move — using a contemporary physicist to validate a Medieval mystic (and vice versa) — is the load-bearing argument of the whole piece and the likely reason it was written for a general 'ideas' audience.
insights.locator: Rovelli's scientific case that we humans

insights.claim: Gardels concludes that consciousness is the perspective of the aware self in a world with no outside, and that the knowing subject is not merely a passive observer of a pre-existing objective reality but its co-creator from within — reality is 'everywhere whole' because there is no vantage point external to it.
insights.speaker: NATHAN GARDELS
insights.so_what: This is the article's thesis statement and title claim: the piece argues for participatory/observer-constitutive realism as the emerging consensus across religion, philosophy and physics — a framework worth citing whenever tracking how 'observer effects' language is used across disciplines (including in AI/consciousness commentary).
insights.quote: Not only is “the universe disclosed by a knowing subject;” the knowing subject is its co-creator from within.
insights.locator: Consciousness, then, can be said to be the perspective
